lessons.title: Displacement, velocity and acceleration
lessons.summary: Use derivatives to calculate velocity and acceleration, find when a particle stops and explain its motion along a straight line.
lessons.objective: Use derivatives to calculate velocity and acceleration, find when a particle stops and explain its motion along a straight line.
lessons.before: Work through the examples with exact values and show the mathematical steps.
lessons.ideas:
A displacement measures position from an origin along the chosen positive direction. Its derivative is the signed velocity \(v=\frac{\mathrm ds}{\mathrm dt}\).

Use \(v=0\) to find a time with no instantaneous motion. Check the permitted time interval and give every valid time.

Differentiate again to obtain \(a=\frac{\mathrm dv}{\mathrm dt}=\frac{\mathrm d^2s}{\mathrm dt^2}\). It measures the change in signed velocity each second.
lessons.method:
How fast is the position changing?

Start by drawing the origin and the positive direction. Differentiate the formula for displacement term by term. A stationary value of the position has velocity zero. The sign of the displacement alone gives a position.

How do I find the times at rest?

Write the velocity equation, factor it where possible and solve each factor. To confirm a reversal, check the sign of velocity before and after the instant.

What does acceleration measure?

Find the velocity expression first. Differentiate it to obtain acceleration and evaluate it at the requested time. Retain a negative result as a signed physical quantity. Compare the signs of velocity and acceleration if asked whether speed increases.
mistakes: A negative displacement puts the particle on the negative side of the origin. Its velocity may still be positive.
An acceleration of zero means the velocity is momentarily unchanged. The velocity may be positive, negative or zero at that time.
When velocity and acceleration are both negative, speed is increasing.

examples.title: Find motion from a position function
examples.question:
A toy train on a straight track has displacement \(s=\frac{t^{2}}{2} - 5 t + 4\) for \(0\le t\le 14\), where t is measured in seconds.

Find the velocity v in terms of t.
examples.solution:
Differentiate each term of the position formula. A constant term has derivative zero.

\(v=t - 5\)

Answer: \(t - 5\).

examples.title: Find motion from a position function
examples.question:
A battery-powered inspection device moves along a straight track. Its position in metres, measured from a fixed reference, is \(s=\frac{7 t^{3}}{3} - \frac{63 t^{2}}{2} + 98 t - 6\) for \(0\le t\le 11\), where t is measured in seconds.

Find the velocity v in terms of t.
examples.solution:
Differentiate each term of the position formula. A constant term has derivative zero.

\(v=7 t^{2} - 63 t + 98\)

Answer: \(7 t^{2} - 63 t + 98\).

examples.title: Read direction from a displacement model
examples.question:
A trolley moves on a straight horizontal rail. Its displacement from the marker is \(s=- 4 t^{2} + 24 t + 10\), in metres, for \(0\le t\le 12\), where t is measured in seconds. Take right as positive.

Find the velocity v in terms of t.
examples.solution:
Differentiate the displacement expression once with respect to time.

\(v=24 - 8 t\)

Answer: \(24 - 8 t\).

lessons.title: Use integration to recover motion
lessons.summary: Integrate acceleration or velocity, use initial conditions to fix constants and calculate changes of position on a specified interval.
lessons.objective: Integrate acceleration or velocity, use initial conditions to fix constants and calculate changes of position on a specified interval.
lessons.before: Work through the examples with exact values and show the mathematical steps.
lessons.ideas:
Integrate acceleration with respect to time. Determine the constant of integration from a known velocity, such as \(v(0)\).

Integrating a known velocity gives an expression for position with its own constant. Use a stated position such as \(s(0)\) to fix that constant.

Integrate signed velocity from the earlier time to the later time. By \(\int_a^b v\,\mathrm dt=s(b)-s(a)\), a fixed origin cancels out.
lessons.method:
How can I recover velocity from acceleration?

Integrate every term of the acceleration and append a constant. Substitute the time and corresponding velocity to determine it. Differentiate your final velocity expression to check that it gives the original acceleration.

What fixes the displacement formula?

First determine the full velocity formula. Integrate that formula, including its constant term. Then substitute the given position and time. If the particle starts at the origin, use zero as its initial position.

How can I find displacement over one interval?

Check whether the question asks for the position at a time or the change between two times. For a change, evaluate the displacement function at both times and subtract in chronological order. A velocity graph gives the same result after adding its areas with signs.
mistakes: An initial velocity can be negative. Keep the sign when substituting the condition.
The constant in the velocity formula gets multiplied by t when you integrate. There is a new constant for displacement.
A question about the displacement from the origin at a given time needs the initial position. The change over an interval does not need it.

examples.title: Recover initial conditions in a motion model
examples.question:
A small robot moves on a straight line. For \(0\le t\le 12\) it has constant acceleration \(10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). It starts at displacement \(-1\,\mathrm{m}\) with velocity \(-40\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

Find an expression for the velocity v at time t.
examples.solution:
An antiderivative of the acceleration is \(10 t\). Use \(v(0)=-40\) to fix the constant.

\(v=10 t - 40\)

Answer: \(10 t - 40\).

examples.title: Recover initial conditions in a motion model
examples.question:
A motor drives a carriage in a straight line. Its acceleration is \(a=8 t - 32\) in metres per second squared for \(0\le t\le 11\). At time zero its velocity is \(27\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and its displacement is \(-3\,\mathrm{m}\).

Find an expression for the velocity v at time t.
examples.solution:
An antiderivative of the acceleration is \(4 t^{2} - 32 t\). Use \(v(0)=27\) to fix the constant.

\(v=4 t^{2} - 32 t + 27\)

Answer: \(4 t^{2} - 32 t + 27\).

examples.title: Recover initial conditions in a motion model
examples.question:
An automated gate moves in a straight line with velocity \(v=1 - 5 t\) in metres per second for \(0\le t\le 7\). At time zero the gate is \(1\,\mathrm{m}\) ahead of its reference marker. The positive direction is forwards.

Find an expression for the displacement s from the origin at time t.
examples.solution:
Integrate \(1 - 5 t\) to obtain the variable part. At time zero the displacement is \(1\,\mathrm{m}\).

\(s=- \frac{5 t^{2}}{2} + t + 1\)

Answer: \(- \frac{5 t^{2}}{2} + t + 1\).

lessons.title: Total distance and changes of direction
lessons.summary: Find times of reversal and use integral intervals to calculate total distance, signed displacement and speed.
lessons.objective: Find times of reversal and use integral intervals to calculate total distance, signed displacement and speed.
lessons.before: Work through the examples with exact values and show the mathematical steps.
lessons.ideas:
Solve \(v=0\) within the model's time range. Check where the sign of v actually changes. Each change separates two directions of motion.

The integral \(\int_a^b v\,\mathrm dt\) measures the net change in position. Parts of the journey in opposite directions can cancel.

Total distance is the area under the speed graph. Compute \(\int_a^b |v|\,\mathrm dt\) by splitting at changes of direction, then adding the magnitudes of the separate displacements.
lessons.method:
Where should I split the time interval?

Factor the velocity to find its zeros. Mark them on a time line with the interval endpoints. Use a single test time in each part to establish the sign of velocity there.

What does the signed integral measure?

Copy the lower and upper limits from the question. Integrate velocity across the entire interval, or sum the signed changes for its separate pieces. Use a graph to check the sign.

How do I calculate total distance?

Use your turning times to create an integral for each time interval. Evaluate each one with its sign, then take its magnitude and add all of them. Equivalently, subtract the smaller position from the larger on every monotone part of the journey.
mistakes: An endpoint or a repeated root can give zero velocity. Check whether the motion reverses within the interval.
The net displacement can be zero after a completed out-and-back journey. The particle still has a positive total distance.
Taking the magnitude of the final net displacement still allows cancellation from earlier stages.

examples.title: Separate total distance and signed displacement
examples.question:
A rail shuttle has velocity \(v=12 t - 84\) in metres per second for \(0\le t\le 12\).

Find all the times at which the particle is at rest.
examples.solution:
Set the signed velocity \(12 t - 84\) equal to zero. Give all roots in the stated time interval.

Answer: \(t=7\).

examples.title: Separate total distance and signed displacement
examples.question:
A sensor travels backwards and forwards along a straight beam. Its velocity in metres per second is \(v=\left(t - 10\right) \left(6 t - 36\right)\) for \(0\le t\le 13\).

Find all the times at which the particle is at rest.
examples.solution:
Set the signed velocity \(\left(t - 10\right) \left(6 t - 36\right)\) equal to zero. Give all roots in the stated time interval.

Answer: \(t=6\text{ or }t=10\).

examples.title: Separate total distance and signed displacement
examples.question:
A model lift has velocity \(v=- 10 \left(t - 5\right) \left(t + 7\right)\) in metres per second for \(0\le t\le 11\). Downwards is the positive direction.

Find all the times at which the particle is at rest.
examples.solution:
Set the signed velocity \(\left(50 - 10 t\right) \left(t + 7\right)\) equal to zero. Give all roots in the stated time interval.

Answer: \(t=5\).

lessons.title: Read and sketch graphs of motion
lessons.summary: Connect and sketch displacement, distance, velocity, speed and acceleration graphs through gradients, signs and areas.
lessons.objective: Connect and sketch displacement, distance, velocity, speed and acceleration graphs through gradients, signs and areas.
lessons.before: Work through the examples with exact values and show the mathematical steps.
lessons.ideas:
A displacement graph with gradient \(v=0\) has a horizontal tangent. An increasing velocity graph has positive acceleration, including where its velocity is negative.

Speed is \(|v|\). Reflect each section of the velocity graph below the time axis to the same height above it. Leave the other parts of the graph in place.

The gradient of the distance graph is \(|v|\). The graph of accumulated distance begins at zero and increases while the particle moves in either direction.
lessons.method:
How do the signed graphs fit together?

Calculate the endpoint values and all relevant zero crossings. Plot velocity before drawing a displacement or acceleration sketch. Use the velocity signs to find increasing and decreasing sections of displacement and use its gradient for acceleration.

How do I draw the speed graph?

Use the velocity graph's times and velocity zeros. Keep those times fixed and reflect only the signs of the negative values. To find distance, add all the areas between the resulting speed graph and the time axis.

What does the distance graph look like?

Plot the initial distance and the distance at each change in direction. The tangent is horizontal when the particle stops. Compare the speed on either side to decide where the distance graph becomes steeper or flatter.
mistakes: A zero on the acceleration graph marks zero velocity gradient. It can occur when the particle has non-zero signed velocity.
A negative area under velocity contributes a positive area under speed after the reflection.
When a particle moves towards the origin, displacement may decrease while total distance continues increasing.

examples.title: Link scale sketches of the motion
examples.question:
A parcel on a testing rail has velocity \(v=4 t - 8\) in metres per second over \(0\le t\le 6\). Its initial displacement from the origin is \(-6\,\mathrm{m}\).

Calculate the velocity when \(t=6\).
examples.solution:
Substitute the final time into \(4 t - 8\). A graph of velocity keeps the sign.

Answer: \(16\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

examples.title: Link scale sketches of the motion
examples.question:
A calibration probe moves along a straight rail with velocity \(v=\left(t - 4\right) \left(7 t - 7\right)\) in metres per second over \(0\le t\le 9\). Its initial displacement is \(0\,\mathrm{m}\).

Calculate the velocity when \(t=9\).
examples.solution:
Substitute the final time into \(\left(t - 4\right) \left(7 t - 7\right)\). A graph of velocity keeps the sign.

Answer: \(280\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

examples.title: Link scale sketches of the motion
examples.question:
A parcel on a testing rail has velocity \(v=5 - t\) in metres per second over \(0\le t\le 9\). Its initial displacement from the origin is \(11\,\mathrm{m}\).

Calculate the velocity when \(t=9\).
examples.solution:
Substitute the final time into \(5 - t\). A graph of velocity keeps the sign.

questions.title: Find motion from a position function
questions.prompt_html:
A toy train on a straight track has displacement \(s=6 t^{2} - 48 t - 2\) for \(0\le t\le 8\), where t is measured in seconds.

  1. Find the velocity v in terms of t.

    [2]

  2. Find all the times at which the particle is at rest.

    [2]

  3. Find the acceleration at \(t=5\).

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Differentiate each term of the position formula. A constant term has derivative zero.

\(v=12 t - 48\)

Answer: \(12 t - 48\).

(b)

Set the signed velocity \(12 t - 48\) equal to zero. Give all roots in the stated time interval.

Answer: \(t=4\).

(c)

Differentiate velocity to get \(a=12\), then substitute the time.

Answer: \(12\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).
questions.hint_html: Take the derivatives in order. The particle is at rest where the first derivative is zero.

marking_criteria.description_html: Apply the power rule to the displacement.
Find every root of the velocity equation in the stated time interval.
Obtain \(t=4\).
Find the derivative of the velocity and evaluate it.
Obtain \(12\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).

A model lift has velocity \(v=- 3 \left(t - 7\right) \left(t + 3\right)\) in metres per second for \(0\le t\le 15\). Downwards is the positive direction.

  1. Find all the times at which the particle is at rest.

    [2]

  2. Find the displacement during \(6\le t\le 15\).

    [2]

  3. Find the total distance travelled during \(6\le t\le 15\).

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Set the signed velocity \(\left(21 - 3 t\right) \left(t + 3\right)\) equal to zero. Give all roots in the stated time interval.

Answer: \(t=7\).

(b)

Evaluate the definite integral of velocity from \(6\,\mathrm{s}\) to \(15\,\mathrm{s}\). Keep the signs of the contributions.

Answer: \(-1458\,\mathrm{m}\).

(c)

Split the time interval at every point where the direction changes.

The signed displacements are from \(6\,\mathrm{s}\) to \(7\,\mathrm{s}\), \(14\,\mathrm{m}\); from \(7\,\mathrm{s}\) to \(15\,\mathrm{s}\), \(-1472\,\mathrm{m}\).

Add the sizes of these displacements to find the total distance travelled.

Answer: \(1486\,\mathrm{m}\).
questions.hint_html: Find every change of direction first. Integrate separately between those times.

marking_criteria.description_html: Find every root of the velocity equation in the stated time interval.
Obtain \(t=7\).
Integrate signed velocity through the entire interval.
Obtain \(-1458\,\mathrm{m}\).
Calculate and sum the absolute displacements on the intervals of fixed direction.
Obtain \(1486\,\mathrm{m}\).

A rail shuttle has velocity \(v=3 t - 9\) in metres per second for \(0\le t\le 13\).

  1. Find all the times at which the particle is at rest.

    [2]

  2. Find the displacement during \(1\le t\le 13\).

    [2]

  3. Find the total distance travelled during \(1\le t\le 13\).

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Set the signed velocity \(3 t - 9\) equal to zero. Give all roots in the stated time interval.

Answer: \(t=3\).

(b)

Evaluate the definite integral of velocity from \(1\,\mathrm{s}\) to \(13\,\mathrm{s}\). Keep the signs of the contributions.

Answer: \(144\,\mathrm{m}\).

(c)

Split the time interval at every point where the direction changes.

The signed displacements are from \(1\,\mathrm{s}\) to \(3\,\mathrm{s}\), \(-6\,\mathrm{m}\); from \(3\,\mathrm{s}\) to \(13\,\mathrm{s}\), \(150\,\mathrm{m}\).

Add the sizes of these displacements to find the total distance travelled.

Answer: \(156\,\mathrm{m}\).
questions.hint_html: Find every change of direction first. Integrate separately between those times.

marking_criteria.description_html: Find every root of the velocity equation in the stated time interval.
Obtain \(t=3\).
Integrate signed velocity through the entire interval.
Obtain \(144\,\mathrm{m}\).
Calculate and sum the absolute displacements on the intervals of fixed direction.
Obtain \(156\,\mathrm{m}\).

A parcel on a testing rail has velocity \(v=12 - 3 t\) in metres per second over \(0\le t\le 10\). Its initial displacement from the origin is \(-5\,\mathrm{m}\).

  1. Calculate the velocity when \(t=10\).

    [2]

  2. Sketch the velocity–time graph. Label both end values and every zero of velocity.

    [2]

  3. Find the distance travelled over the whole interval.

    [2]

  4. Sketch the graph of accumulated distance against time. Label the distances when the particle first comes to rest and at the end of the interval.

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a) \(-18\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\)

(b) Velocity starts at \(12\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), crosses its axis at \(4\,\mathrm{s}\), and ends at \(-18\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

(c) \(78\,\mathrm{m}\)

(d) The graph increases to \(24\,\mathrm{m}\) at \(4\,\mathrm{s}\), with a horizontal tangent there, then continues increasing.
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Substitute the final time into \(12 - 3 t\). A graph of velocity keeps the sign.

Answer: \(-18\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

(b)

Set \(v=12 - 3 t\) equal to zero to locate the intercepts. The graph is a straight line.

(c)

The velocity graph gives signed triangular areas \(24\,\mathrm{m}\) and \(-54\,\mathrm{m}\). Add their magnitudes.

Answer: \(78\,\mathrm{m}\).

(d)

Use the slope of the distance graph to represent the speed. The slope decreases to zero and then increases again.
questions.hint_html: Velocity supplies the signed rate of change of position. Absolute velocity supplies speed.

marking_criteria.description_html: Evaluate the given velocity at the final time.
Calculate initial and final velocities and find the zeros of the velocity.
Draw the correct shape passing through the labelled end values and through zero at \(4\,\mathrm{s}\).
Use both areas and take their magnitudes before adding.
Obtain \(78\,\mathrm{m}\).
Use speed as the gradient and zero initial distance.
Show increasing branches on both sides of \(4\,\mathrm{s}\) with the correct distance there.
Show the horizontal tangent at the change of direction and reach \(78\,\mathrm{m}\) at the final time.
